claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has moderate or relatively low hardness and strength but high ductility.
The mechanical-property combination is governed mainly by the absence of precipitation, ordering, or other additional strengthening mechanisms.
The constituent elements have sufficiently balanced atomic sizes to produce only modest solid-solution strengthening.
Modest solid-solution strengthening leaves dislocation motion relatively unimpeded.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation motion causes lower hardness and strength together with greater plasticity.
Precipitation or ordering in related high-entropy alloy systems impedes dislocations, increases hardness and strength, and reduces ductility.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can yield single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with no detectable secondary phases.
The proposed single-phase solid solution may be either FCC or BCC.
Aging equimolar CoCrFeNiTi at 600 °C for 24 hours under inert atmosphere will induce fine precipitates or ordered regions.
Fine secondary phases or ordered regions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The homogeneous simple solid solution lacks significant lattice distortion and precipitate obstacles.
Aging-induced dislocation pinning increases hardness and strength.
Aged, precipitate-containing CoCrFeNiTi will have greater hardness than the homogeneous control at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
Aged, precipitate-containing CoCrFeNiTi will have greater compressive strength than the homogeneous control at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
Aged, precipitate-containing CoCrFeNiTi will have lower plastic strain than the homogeneous control at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi initially processed as a single phase and tested at temperatures no higher than 600 °C.
Grain size and residual stress may also affect the deformation behavior.

contradictions.description: The control is alternately described as homogenized and as-cast. A sample that has undergone post-casting homogenization is not strictly in the as-cast state, so the baseline processing history is internally inconsistent.
